title: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad

segments.voice: Then two weeks of the peace chants, day six. Yesterday, apyayantu: strong limbs first, and no turning away, from either side. Today's chant asks the mouth and the mind to stop pulling in two directions.

Sounds great, someone types, while thinking the exact opposite. The words go one way; the mind goes another. The peace chant of the Aitareya Upanishad treats that split as serious enough to name first. And it sits right on top of an old argument inside the tradition: in a sacred chant, what matters more, the exact sound or the understanding?
screen: `'SOUNDS GREAT.'` → `WORDS ONE WAY, MIND ANOTHER.` → `SOUND, OR UNDERSTANDING?`

segments.voice: The chant is known by its first words, van me manasi. In plain words: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind rooted in my speech. Speech and mind, bring me the Veda. May what I have heard not leave me. I will speak what is right. I will speak what is true. May that protect me, and protect the one who speaks. Then: Om, peace, peace, peace. Now the argument, and both sides get to speak. First, the reciters. Students learned the Vedas by ear, with methods built to keep every syllable exactly as it was handed down, because the sound itself is held sacred. A chant said exactly is already an offering, understood or not, and it keeps the text alive for the next person who will understand it. Second, the interpreters. Yaska, an early teacher of what Vedic words mean, compares someone who recites the Veda without knowing its meaning to a post carrying a load: it bears the weight and gets nothing from it. And the chant itself? It holds both. It wants the words exact: what is right, what is true. And it wants them rooted in the mind.
screen: `SPEECH ROOTED IN MIND.` · `THE RECITERS: THE SOUND IS SACRED.` · `YASKA: A POST CARRYING A LOAD.` · then, large: `THE CHANT HOLDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Choose one true sentence you could say about today, short and plain, and say it out loud, slowly, meaning each word as it leaves you. Then say it once more, softer. Let the rest of the sit be quiet, words and mind standing in the same place.
The peace chants, and today van me manasi: may my speech be rooted in my mind, and my mind in my speech.
Something to keep: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad, words and mind in one place. Same time tomorrow.
